title: Permutations
tagline: Place each unused element in turn — generate all n! orderings.

intuition.analogy: Seating n guests in a row: choose anyone for seat 1, then anyone remaining for seat 2, and so on. The number of ways is n × (n−1) × … × 1 = n!.
paragraphs: A permutation is an ordering of all elements. Backtracking builds one position at a time: for the current slot, try every element not yet used, recurse, then mark it unused again (backtrack).
A 'used' boolean array (or in-place swapping) prevents reusing an element. When the current arrangement has length n, it's a complete permutation to record.
Unlike subsets (binary choices), permutations branch n-ways at the top, (n−1)-ways next, etc., yielding the factorial explosion — so they're only practical for small n.
intuition.keyIdea: Fill positions left to right, trying each unused element; backtrack by freeing the element after recursing.

steps.title: Track usage
steps.detail: Maintain a used[] flag (or swap elements into place) so each element appears once per permutation.

steps.title: Choose and recurse
steps.detail: For each unused element, mark it used, append to current, recurse; then unmark and pop (backtrack).

steps.title: Record full-length arrangements
steps.detail: When current has n elements, store a copy.

complexity.timeReason: n! permutations, each O(n) to build/copy.
complexity.spaceReason: Recursion depth and the used/current arrays.

pitfalls: Skipping the 'unmark used' step leaks state across branches.
For duplicates, sort and skip equal unused siblings to avoid repeats.
Copy the current arrangement when recording, not the live reference.

dryRun.clickMoment: The branching factor shrinks each level: 3 choices, then 2, then 1 — exactly the n! count. Backtracking systematically reuses freed elements down each new branch.
